displayQuote: Never argue with stupid people, they will drag you down to their level and beat you with experience

meta.title: Who really said "Never argue with stupid people"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Twain — the attribution only appears in 2009, a century after he died. The earliest version is from 1956, where Yul Brynner credited it to his friend Jean Cocteau, and 'beat you with experience' is a much later mutation.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Never argue with stupid people'?
meta.ogDescription: No Twain source at all; the credit surfaces on social media in 2009. The 1956 original was credited by Yul Brynner to Jean Cocteau — and said 'idiots', not 'stupid people'.

answer.label: Not Twain — credited to Jean Cocteau by Yul Brynner, 1956
answer.sourceLine: There is no Twain source of any kind — the attribution does not appear in print at all, and surfaces on social media only around 2009, ninety-nine years after he died. The oldest version we can date is from 13 November 1956, in a news profile of the actor Yul Brynner, who was asked for the best advice he had ever received and credited his friend Jean Cocteau.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Associated Press profile of Yul Brynner

source.excerpt: Never associate with idiots on their own level, because, being an intelligent man, you'll try to deal with them on their level — and on their level they'll beat you every time.
trail: The oldest datable form is the 1956 Brynner profile, where the advice is ‘never associate with idiots on their own level’ and is credited to Cocteau. Note it is about associating, not arguing Quote Investigator ↗.

The ‘argue’ wording appears in a student newspaper on 15 January 1958: ‘Never argue with an idiot, because being an intelligent man, you will argue with them on their level, and, on their level, they’ll beat you every time.’ Cocteau credits persist in newspapers into the 1980s.

The Twain attribution has no print history at all. It appears on Twitter around June 2009 and is standard on quote-aggregator sites by the early 2010s — the Center for Mark Twain Studies files it among the apocryphal Apocryphal Twain ↗.
source.excerptNote: The 1956 wording. Everything memorable about the modern version — ‘drag you down to their level,’ ‘beat you with experience’ — came later; the punchline in 1956 is simply ‘they’ll beat you every time.’

source.rightsNote: No Twain basis, so there is no public-domain claim here — a common and costly assumption, since people reproduce ‘Twain’ quotes commercially on the belief that anything of his is free. The real chain is modern: Jean Cocteau died in 1963, so his work is under French copyright into the 2030s, and the 1956 newspaper text’s US status is unresolved. Quote the 1956 line briefly with attribution rather than reproducing it as free content. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Mark Twain
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Twain
author.bio: Mark Twain is the default author for any American-sounding wisecrack, to the point that the Center for Mark Twain Studies runs a standing series cataloguing things he never said. This one is a clear case of the mechanism: a 1950s piece of advice about idiots circulated for fifty years under other names, then acquired Twain’s in the social-media era, when a punchy line needs an author and nobody checks.

copyAttribution: Not Mark Twain. The 1956 original: "Never associate with idiots on their own level… on their level they'll beat you every time." —Jean Cocteau, as recalled by Yul Brynner.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: This one is unusually clean to date, because the Twain credit has no print history whatsoever — it begins on social media, and we can watch the wording mutate before it gets there.

items.why: There is no printed Twain attribution at any point. It surfaces on Twitter around 2009 and becomes standard on quote sites by the early 2010s — ninety-nine years after his death Twain Studies ↗.
The 1956 line ends ‘they’ll beat you every time.’ ‘Drag you down to their level’ and ‘beat you with experience’ have no 1950s antecedent — they are later improvements to somebody else’s advice.

We report Cocteau because a named associate credited him in print in 1956 — but researchers have not located the remark in Cocteau’s own published writing, and the English we have is Brynner’s rendering. Treat it as the best-documented attribution, not a verified one.

misattribution.truthLine: Not Twain in any form. The oldest version is from 1956, where Yul Brynner credited Jean Cocteau — and the modern wording is a later mutation of that full chain ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: It offers a dignified exit from an argument you are losing, and flatters the person quoting it as the intelligent party by construction. That is a lot of work for one sentence, which is why it has been improved so many times.

The 1956 version is narrower and more useful: do not associate with fools on their own terms, because the terms are the trap. Turning ‘associate’ into ‘argue’ converted a caution about company into a licence to walk away from disagreement.
detailsBody: 1956, Brynner citing Cocteau: ‘Never associate with idiots on their own level… on their level they’ll beat you every time.’
1958, student newspaper: ‘Never argue with an idiot…’ — the verb changes.
Into the 1980s: still credited to Cocteau in the press.
c. 2009: appears on Twitter as Mark Twain; standard on quote sites by the early 2010s.
Also credited along the way to George Carlin.
context.pull: The Twain credit has no print history at all. It starts on Twitter in 2009.
